failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM651.955-958 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Wear (TSB LI80.20-P-050001)
items.whatHappens: The early OM651 timing chain tensioner can fail, leading to chain slack, a distinct metallic rattle on cold starts, and potentially catastrophic valve-to-piston contact if the chain jumps a tooth.
items.repairVsReplace: Mercedes issued an updated tensioner design to resolve this. If caught early, replacing the tensioner and chain is cost-effective. If valve damage has already occurred, a full reconditioned OM651 unit is required.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death")
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the injectors degrade, allowing high-pressure combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads, leading to a distinct tapping noise, rough idling, and a strong smell of exhaust in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: DPF and EGR Clogging (Commercial Use)
items.whatHappens: Urban delivery patterns and frequent short trips cause excessive soot buildup in the EGR valve and Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF), leading to restricted airflow, limp mode, and increased backpressure that can prematurely wear the turbocharger.
items.repairVsReplace: Professional DPF cleaning or EGR replacement is a standard repair. If the turbocharger has suffered damage from prolonged backpressure, a full turbo rebuild or replacement is necessary.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2011 units with the updated timing chain tensioner and revised ECU mapping show significantly fewer catastrophic chain failures, making them the most desirable examples of this engine family .

variants.title: OM651.955-958 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Van?
variants.intro: INTRO: The OM651 family fragments into numerous raw sub-codes. The .955 through .958 variants are specifically calibrated for commercial van applications, differing primarily by power output, transmission pairing, and heavy-duty ancillary mounting. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting a passenger-car spec engine into a commercial van will lead to immediate mounting and drivetrain incompatibility. - Fitted to: Sprinter 906 (211 CDI, 311 CDI, 511 CDI) - Key technical difference: The entry-level commercial tune, featuring a smaller turbocharger and specific ECU mapping optimized for low-end torque and fuel economy in light-duty urban delivery. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; no unique widespread defects beyond the standard tensioner and seal issues. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the higher-output .957/.958 variants; the turbo plumbing, ECU, and wiring loom are entirely different. - Fitted to: Vito / Viano W639 (113 CDI) - Key technical difference: A mid-range output tune specifically developed for the W639 Vito/Viano platform, balancing payload capacity with acceptable fuel consumption. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. - Interchange note: Requires matching W639-specific engine mounts, sump, and accessory drives; not directly interchangeable with Sprinter variants. - Fitted to: Sprinter 906 (213 CDI, 313 CDI, 513 CDI), Vito / Viano W639 (116 CDI) - Key technical difference: The volume-seller mid-to-high output variant, featuring a variable-geometry turbocharger (VGT) and revised piston cooling jets to handle the increased thermal load of heavier payloads. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; VGT actuator wear is slightly more prevalent due to higher boost loads. - Interchange note: The Sprinter and Vito versions share the core block, but the oil pickup, sump, and flywheel are application-specific and not directly interchangeable without modification. - Fitted to: Sprinter 906 (216 CDI, 316 CDI, 516 CDI) - Key technical difference: The highest output commercial variant, featuring a larger turbocharger, upgraded intercooler, and reinforced internal components to handle the demands of high-speed motorway cruising and maximum payload towing. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; turbocharger seal wear and DPF clogging are more prevalent due to the higher thermal and soot loads. - Interchange note: Cannot be swapped with the .955/.957 without significant ECU, wiring loom, and turbo plumbing changes.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM651.955-958 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: When searching for a used OM651.955-958 engine for sale, it makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented replacement of the timing chain tensioner and injector seals. Given the catastrophic risk of chain failure in commercial use, buying a used unit with unknown history is a significant financial risk.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM651 engine is the sweet spot for most fleet and commercial buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by installing the updated timing chain tensioner, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the EGR/DPF components, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM651 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage Sprinter or Vito hosts where maximum longevity and minimal downtime are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM651 engine is installed by specialists familiar with Mercedes commercial CDI systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM651 is typically found in Sprinter and Vito vehicles valued between £5,000 and £18,000, a full replacement is generally financially viable and comfortably within the host vehicle's value . Replacement cost rarely exceeds the scrap threshold for these chassis, making a reconditioned unit a highly sensible investment for commercial operators.

items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM651.955-958 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are timing chain tensioner wear (addressed under TSB LI80.20-P-050001), injector seal weeping ("Black Death"), and DPF/EGR clogging. The timing chain tensioner can fail and cause catastrophic valve damage if ignored, while injector seal failure causes black carbon buildup but is a cheap preventative fix. items.answer: A reconditioned OM651.955-958 is strongly recommended over a used unit for commercial use. A proper rebuild will proactively address the fatal flaw by installing the updated timing chain tensioner, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the EGR/DPF components, whereas a used engine with unknown history risks immediate catastrophic chain failure and costly vehicle downtime. items.question: What is the difference between OM651.955, .956, .957, and .958?
items.answer: The OM651.955 is the entry-level 88-120 hp tune, the .956 is the 109 hp Vito-specific variant, the .957 is the volume-seller 129-136 hp variant with a variable-geometry turbo, and the .958 is the highest-output 163 hp variant for heavy-duty Sprinter applications. They share the same core block, but the turbo plumbing, ECU mapping, and accessory drives differ significantly.
